questions.q: What is the stated goal of this capstone?
options: To memorize every lesson title from Chapters 1-4
To pick the shortest possible use case to minimize effort
To prove you can build a tested, versioned, genuinely evaluated prompt library around a real use case of your own choosing
To rewrite the course outline file
questions.explain: The kickoff frames the capstone as applying the course's full pipeline — prompts, context, and evaluation — to a real use case, producing real results rather than a guided walkthrough.

questions.q: According to the deliverable list, what must deliverable #4 (the token budget) include?
options: An output reserve, fixed costs, and capped variable costs — the worksheet shape from Lesson 13
Only a total token count with no further breakdown
A list of every model vendor's pricing
A single screenshot of a token counter tool
questions.explain: The brief explicitly ties this deliverable back to Lesson 13's budgeting worksheet: output reserve, fixed costs, and capped variable costs.

questions.q: Under what condition does the brief say the tool-description deliverable can be skipped?
options: It can never be skipped under any circumstances
If the student runs out of time
If the system prompt is already long enough
If the chosen use case genuinely has no tool calls
questions.explain: The deliverable list states this requirement applies only if the use case calls a tool — otherwise it's not applicable and can be skipped honestly.

questions.q: What does deliverable #9 (the A/B comparison) require, according to the brief?
options: Testing ten unrelated prompts against each other simultaneously
One prompt variable changed, tested on the same eval set, with a documented winner and a specific reason
Changing as many prompt variables as possible at once for thoroughness
Skipping the eval set entirely and relying on intuition
questions.explain: This directly reflects Lesson 20's A/B testing discipline: isolate one variable, test fairly on the same eval set, and document a specific reason for the winner.

questions.q: What does the lesson's "realistic order of operations" recommend doing before the A/B comparison and regression baseline?
options: Nothing — those should be done first, before writing any prompts
Skipping prompt-writing entirely and going straight to regression testing
Getting the use case, prompts, context budget, ordering, and eval set/testing working first, since A/B and regression both need a working, tested baseline to compare against
Choosing the use case only after the regression baseline is set
questions.explain: The lesson explains that A/B testing and regression baselining require something stable and already tested to compare against, so they come after the use case, prompts, context work, and eval set are in place.
